frus-1861-d7:
On 15 May 1861, Joseph Wright sent a further dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is document 7 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A week between letters tells of a post reporting on a steady rhythm. Wright wrote as Britain and France weighed how to treat the warring American states. His dispatches gave Seward raw fact and local talk to weigh against reports from grander capitals. Steady weekly reports built the trust that let a small post speak with a clear voice. A steady hand at a small post freed the great posts to take the larger risks.
frus-1862-d7:
Another report crossed the ocean to Seward, this one from Charles Francis Adams on 17 January 1862. It stands as Document 7 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the winter of the war's second year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Inbound reports like this one told Washington what its man abroad saw, heard, and judged. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d7:
On 21 November 1862, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from the legation in London. The date falls out of line with the letters around it in the printed volume. The dispatch is document 7 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Printed files do not always run in strict date order, since enclosures and late mail were set where they fit. The letter is Adams's work all the same: a report from the post that watched Britain's stance toward the war. Read with its mates, it helps fill the last weeks of November 1862 at the London legation.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d7: Stalin wrote back to Roosevelt on June 11, 1943, and his message is Document 7 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. June brought hard bargaining between the allies over the timing of the invasion of France, though this record names no subject for the letter itself. It sits in the published run of letters that slowly arranged the Tehran summit. The State Department printed it in the Foreign Relations series, the official history of American diplomacy.
frus-1944-quebec-d7:
Prime Minister Churchill followed up with another message to President Roosevelt on May 28, 1944, the third in four days. The State Department printed it in the Quebec 1944 volume's pre-conference papers.

Churchill's late-May letters came as the invasion fleet waited on the weather and the final orders. He wrote to fix details, argue priorities, and keep his influence on decisions that American power increasingly shaped. For readers, the message shows the Prime Minister working his one indispensable channel at the moment of maximum strain, days before the alliance's greatest gamble in France.
frus-1945-50-intel-d7:
Edward Tamm, Hoover's closest assistant at the FBI, sent an inside memorandum to Hoover on 6 September 1945. Tamm handled much of the bureau's contact with the rest of the government. It is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the retrospective volume on American intelligence from 1945 to 1950.

Inside memoranda show what an agency said to itself, which can differ from what it said to rivals. Tamm's paper gives readers the FBI's private view at the moment the postwar intelligence fight was taking shape. Hoover ran his bureau through a small circle of trusted men, and Tamm stood at its center. Papers from that circle, printed here, let readers hear the bureau thinking aloud about threats to its power and plans to meet them.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d7: President Roosevelt directed this message to Ambassador Harriman in Moscow on 4 October 1944. Kept as document 7 in the Foreign Relations volume on Malta and Yalta, it shows the president instructing his envoy rather than receiving reports. Instructions of this kind told Harriman what line to take with Soviet officials during the months of preparation before the Yalta Conference met.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d7:
Roosevelt had promised to visit England; Churchill asked Truman to keep the promise in this telegram of May 13, 1945. The late President had pledged to come before going to France — or, as it had now become, Germany. Britain would feel disappointed, Churchill writes, if Truman did not come. But ceremony must not disturb the sequence of events.

The conference of the three should come as soon and wherever possible, he argues — perhaps in June, if Truman's fiscal year allows. Both ambassadors should do their utmost to induce Stalin to propose the meeting, and London would instruct accordingly. England could wait; the summit could not.
tob-0039-d7:
Roll 8 belongs to the microfilm transcript of the Doctors' Trial, the Nuremberg proceedings of 1946 to 1947 against physicians of the Third Reich. The case grew out of experiments in concentration camps, where prisoners were used as test subjects. Seven defendants would hang at the end of it.

Within this roll, the tribunal works on through testimony, affidavits, and exhibits, in the flat language of a court at work. That flatness matters: it is evidence, not commentary, preserved whole. The complete transcript underlies every history of the trial and of the Nuremberg Code that came out of it. Roll by roll, the set stands as the trial's own memory of itself.
